thesis: AI agents in 2020-2025 primarily automate routine cognitive tasks while raising demand for complementary tasks of supervision, orchestration, and judgment, so their employment effect is a structural restructuring of tasks within jobs rather than aggregate net job destruction; the net effect depends on the relative pace of task automatability versus complementary-task demand.

positions.name: Augmentation & new-work reinstatement
positions.gist: Technology displaces some tasks but historically complements labor and creates entirely new tasks and occupations, so the reinstatement effect and new-work creation broadly offset displacement and can raise demand for less-skilled workers.

positions.name: Task displacement & falling labor share
positions.gist: Automation shifts the task content of production against labor and always reduces the labor share, and recent so-so automation displaces workers faster than reinstatement creates new tasks, so net labor demand can fall even as productivity rises.

positions.name: Mass automatability (occupation-level)
positions.gist: A machine-learning assessment of whole occupations finds a very large share of jobs are highly susceptible to computerisation, implying broad displacement risk concentrated in routine, low-wage, low-education work.

positions.name: Task-based low-automatability revision
positions.gist: Because jobs bundle many hard-to-automate tasks, an occupation-level count overstates risk; a task-based approach finds only a small share of jobs are fully automatable on average across OECD countries, implying restructuring rather than wholesale destruction.

positions.name: Broad general-purpose exposure skewed to high-skill
positions.gist: LLMs behave like a general-purpose technology whose task exposure spans most of the workforce and, unlike prior automation, rises with income and education rather than concentrating on low-skill routine work.

positions.name: Polarization / distributional hollowing-out
positions.gist: Routine-biased technological change and offshoring hollow out middle-skill routine jobs while expanding high-skill and low-skill service employment, so the effect is distributional job and wage polarization rather than uniform net destruction.

positions.name: Diffusion-lag / productivity J-curve / null-effects
positions.gist: General-purpose technologies need complementary intangible investment before payoffs appear, so measured near-term labor-market effects of generative AI are precise zeros and any large employment impact is delayed, not absent.

positions.name: Post-work / structural unemployment & redistribution
positions.gist: Cumulative automation will eventually leave not enough work for everyone, producing structural technological unemployment that markets will not self-correct and that requires redistribution such as a basic income.

benchmark_claims.claim: Share of US employment at high risk of computerisation (occupation-level, 702 occupations)
Share of jobs automatable on average across 21 OECD countries (task-based)
Share of US workforce with >=10 percent / >=50 percent of tasks exposed to LLMs
benchmark_claims.value: about 80 percent (>=10 percent); about 19 percent (>=50 percent)

benchmark_claims.claim: Productivity effect of a generative-AI assistant on customer-support agents
benchmark_claims.value: +14 percent on average; +34 percent for novice/low-skilled; minimal for experienced

benchmark_claims.claim: Effect of AI chatbots on earnings/hours across 11 exposed occupations in Denmark
benchmark_claims.value: precise zeros, CIs ruling out effects larger than 1 percent; average time savings 2.8 percent

benchmark_claims.claim: Share of US wage-structure change over four decades from routine-task workers' relative wage declines
Understatement of US TFP when adjusting for intangible complements (productivity J-curve)
benchmark_claims.value: TFP level 15.9 percent higher than official measures by end of 2017

benchmark_claims.claim: Scope over which pervasive job polarization is documented
Contribution of newly created work to present-day employment (1940-2018)
benchmark_claims.value: the majority of current employment is in new job specialties introduced after 1940
